transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name]. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I’ve been… I don’t know, blowing up at people over nothing. Like, I’m a general operations manager, so I’m on calls all the time, and lately I’ll be on an operations call and someone will ask a normal question or miss some detail, and I just snap. I hear myself getting sharp, raising my voice, cutting people off, and it’s like I’m already angry before I’ve even had time to think.

And it’s not just work, which is the part that’s really bothering me. I’m doing it at home too, with my family. Small stuff—things I would normally just handle or let go—I’m reacting like it’s some huge problem. That’s not how I’ve ever been. I mean, I’ve dealt with pressure before, that’s basically my job, but this feels different. I don’t like who I’m turning into, and I figured I needed to come in before I damage something I can’t fix.
Have you gone through any major changes, stressors, or difficult life events around the time when you started noticing these changes in your mood and reactions?

Yeah… yes. It started right after something happened at the facility. There was a valve failure, and someone got injured. That was about three weeks ago now, I think—maybe just over, but around three weeks.

And since then, it’s like everything in me has been wound too tight. Before that happened, I was under stress like anybody in operations is, but I could manage it. After the valve failed and the injury happened, that’s when I started noticing I wasn’t reacting like myself anymore. It’s hard because I keep going back over it in my head, thinking about the timing, and it really does line up almost exactly with that incident.

Since the incident at work, have you noticed that your anger or irritability is often out of proportion to the actual situation, like overreacting to small things that wouldn’t have bothered you before?

Yes. That’s exactly what scares me about it, honestly. It’s not like I’m getting irritated because something truly major is happening in that moment. It’s more like… someone asks a routine question on an operations call, or misses a detail, or something at home doesn’t go the way I expected, and I react like they’ve done something terrible.

I’ll snap, cut people off, raise my voice—sometimes before I’ve even really processed what they said. And then afterward I’m sitting there thinking, why did I come down that hard? I’ve handled high-pressure situations for years, and I’m used to people making mistakes or needing clarification. That’s part of the job. But lately it’s like my fuse is gone. I keep blowing up over things that I know, rationally, are small.

And it’s happening with my family too, which makes me feel worse. They’ll do something normal—nothing that should set me off—and I’ll answer sharply or get angry, and then I can see the look on their faces. That’s not me. Or at least it wasn’t. So yes, it’s definitely out of proportion. I know it is, and I still can’t seem to stop it fast enough.
Has your irritability or anger been happening even when there isn’t a specific stressor or trigger present, like you’re just walking around feeling on edge or ready to snap?

Yeah… I think so. It’s not always like there’s one clear thing that sets it off. A lot of the time I’m just already walking around with this… edge to me, like I’m braced for somebody to say the wrong thing or make one small mistake, and then I’m snapping before I even realize I’m doing it.

At work, I’ll get on an operations call and I can feel myself tense before anyone has even really done anything. Then someone asks a normal question, or misses some small detail, and I blow up like it’s this huge failure. And at home it’s similar—my family isn’t doing anything wrong, not really, but I’ll answer sharply or get irritated over nothing.

That’s the part that doesn’t feel like me. I’m used to handling pressure. I’ve always had to keep my head in stressful situations. But lately it’s like I’m carrying the anger around with me, and the trigger is almost just an excuse for it to come out.
Have you noticed any changes in your mood, like feeling down or losing interest in things you usually enjoy, since the incident at work?

Yeah… I have noticed that. It’s not exactly like I’m crying all the time or anything, but I don’t feel like myself emotionally. It’s like the part of me that should be able to feel good things just doesn’t really switch on.

At home, my wife will make dinner, or the kids will be talking about soccer, just normal family stuff, and I know I should feel glad to be there. I know that. I can look at it and think, this is a good moment, this is the kind of thing I’m supposed to enjoy. But inside it’s like there’s nothing there that can respond. I’m sitting at the table, hearing them talk, and I’m present physically, but I feel kind of cut off from it.

And that bothers me because those are usually the things that ground me. My family, the regular routines, hearing about the kids’ games or whatever happened at practice—that should make me feel something. But since the incident, it’s like I’m just going through the motions and watching everyone else have a normal evening while I’m… not able to connect to it the way I should.
Have you been feeling down or losing interest in activities you usually enjoy most days, even when there isn’t a specific stressor happening?

Yes… most days, I’d say. Even when nothing is actively happening, even when it should be a normal evening, I still feel kind of shut off from the things I’d normally enjoy.

Like my wife will make dinner, or my kids will be talking about soccer, just regular family stuff, and I know I should feel glad to be there. I can recognize it in my head, like, this is good, this is what matters, this is the kind of thing I usually care about. But it’s like there’s nothing in me that can respond to it. I’m there, I’m listening, I’m looking at them, but I don’t feel connected to it the way I should.

And that’s been really hard, because it’s not like something specific has to set it off. It’s just… there. Even in quiet moments, even when things are actually fine, I feel like I’m going through the motions instead of feeling happy or settled with them.
Have you noticed that you’ve been feeling unusually tired or lacking energy most days, even when you haven’t been doing anything physically demanding?

I’m… not really sure how to answer that one. I mean, I’m tired sometimes, but I don’t know if I’d say it’s this separate thing where I’m physically drained most days for no reason.

I haven’t been tracking it that way, I guess. Some days I feel worn out, but I can’t tell if that’s just from everything feeling heavy mentally, or from not relaxing the way I normally would, or just normal work and family stuff piling up. It’s not like I’ve noticed myself unable to get up off the couch or anything clear like that.

So… I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure. I’ve noticed feeling off, definitely, but the low-energy part specifically? I don’t know. I’d have to think about that more.
Have you noticed that you’re not getting pleasure or satisfaction out of things that you usually enjoy, even when you’re doing them?

Yeah… yes, that’s exactly what I mean. I can still do the things, technically. I can sit at dinner with my wife, I can listen to the kids talk about soccer, ask them how practice was, nod along, all of that. From the outside it probably looks like I’m participating.

But inside, it’s like… nothing lands. My wife will make dinner, and normally I’d feel grateful or comfortable, just happy to be home with everyone. Or the kids will start going on about a game or who scored or something funny that happened, and I know that should make me smile for real. I know I should feel glad to be there with them.

But it’s like there’s nothing in me that can respond. I’m hearing it, I understand it, I know it matters to me, but I don’t get that warmth or satisfaction from it. It feels like I’m watching the moment happen instead of actually being part of it. And that’s… that’s really hard, because those are the things I usually enjoy the most.
Have these feelings of being emotionally disconnected, losing pleasure in things you usually enjoy, and feeling down been present almost every day since the incident at work?

Yes… yes, pretty much every day. I mean, I keep trying to tell myself maybe I’m just having a bad day, or maybe if the evening goes normally I’ll snap back into it, but it hasn’t really been like that.

It’s there even during the regular family moments. My wife will make dinner, or the kids will be talking about soccer, just normal stuff that should make me feel glad to be home with them. And I know, in my head, that I should feel something good there. I know I love them, I know those moments matter to me. But it’s like there’s nothing in me that can respond the way it used to.

I’ll be sitting there listening, trying to be present, and I’m aware that this should feel comforting or happy or at least normal… but it just doesn’t reach me. It feels like I’m cut off from the part of me that would usually feel that. And that’s been happening almost every day since then, yeah.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep, like trouble falling asleep, waking up during the night, or sleeping much more than usual, nearly every day since the incident?

Yeah… sleep has been really bad. Almost every night, honestly. I’ll get into bed and I’ll be exhausted, like I should just be able to pass out, but then as soon as it’s quiet my mind just… goes right back there.

I keep hearing the alarm in my head. Not like I think it’s actually happening in the room, but it’s so clear that my body reacts like it is. I’ll be lying there staring at the ceiling, trying to tell myself I’m home, I’m in bed, everything is fine, but I can still hear it, and then I’m tense all over. It can take forever before I actually drift off.

And when I do sleep, it doesn’t feel like real sleep. I wake up sweating from dreams about the smoke and people yelling. Sometimes I wake up so suddenly that for a second I don’t even know where I am, and then I’m just lying there trying to calm down. After that it’s hard to fall back asleep because I’m almost waiting for it to happen again.

So by morning, I feel like I barely slept at all. Even if I was technically in bed for hours, it doesn’t feel restful. It’s been most nights since the incident, yeah.

I’ll be sitting there listening, trying to be present, and I’m aware that this should feel comforting or happy or at least normal… but it just doesn’t reach me. It feels like I’m cut off from the part of me that would usually feel that. And that’s been happening almost every day since then, yeah.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant change in sleep patterns (insomnia or hypersomnia) nearly every day since the incident, which would help differentiate between the current candidate diagnoses.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your sleep, like trouble falling asleep, waking up during the night, or sleeping much more than usual, nearly every day since the incident?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: Most nights I lie there hearing that alarm in my head, and when I finally doze off I wake up sweating from dreams about smoke and people yelling, so by morning I feel like I never slept at all.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about changes in sleep, including trouble falling asleep, waking during the night, or sleeping more than usual since the incident.

patient.answer:
Yeah… sleep has been really bad. Almost every night, honestly. I’ll get into bed and I’ll be exhausted, like I should just be able to pass out, but then as soon as it’s quiet my mind just… goes right back there.

I keep hearing the alarm in my head. Not like I think it’s actually happening in the room, but it’s so clear that my body reacts like it is. I’ll be lying there staring at the ceiling, trying to tell myself I’m home, I’m in bed, everything is fine, but I can still hear it, and then I’m tense all over. It can take forever before I actually drift off.

And when I do sleep, it doesn’t feel like real sleep. I wake up sweating from dreams about the smoke and people yelling. Sometimes I wake up so suddenly that for a second I don’t even know where I am, and then I’m just lying there trying to calm down. After that it’s hard to fall back asleep because I’m almost waiting for it to happen again.

So by morning, I feel like I barely slept at all. Even if I was technically in bed for hours, it doesn’t feel restful. It’s been most nights since the incident, yeah.

inference.note: This turn confirmed persistent depressive symptoms nearly every day since the incident, loss of pleasure in activities, emotional detachment, and significant sleep disturbances including nightmares and re-experiencing the traumatic event during sleep. This supports the presence of a major depressive episode, likely severe (F32.3 or F33.3 if recurrent). Other candidates (F32.2, F33.2) were ruled out due to the severity and persistence of symptoms and the presence of trauma-related features.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a major depressive episode occurring in the context of a recurrent depressive disorder, with onset linked to a traumatic workplace incident approximately three weeks ago. Symptoms include persistent depressed mood, loss of interest and pleasure in usual activities, irritability disproportionate to situational triggers, emotional numbing, sleep disturbance with nightmares, and functional impairment across work and home settings. Although the timing could suggest an adjustment disorder with depressed mood, the severity, pervasiveness, and persistence of symptoms beyond what would be expected in response to a stressor support a diagnosis of recurrent major depressive disorder, moderate to severe.
